theme: Jacob’s blessings; Judah’s primacy; Joseph’s death
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 48:1-50:26. The final three chapters of Genesis. Jacob blesses Joseph’s sons and then blesses all twelve of his own sons in a prophetic poem. He dies and is buried in Canaan. Joseph forgives his brothers a final time. Genesis ends with his bones in a coffin in Egypt, awaiting the return to the promised land.
settingTheScene: We have come to the end of Genesis. Jacob, near death, calls Joseph to him and blesses Joseph’s two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, crossing his hands so that the younger receives the greater blessing. Then in chapter 49 he summons all twelve sons and prophesies their futures. The blessing on Judah is particularly significant, a scepter will not depart from him until the one to whom it belongs comes. Jacob dies. Joseph and the brothers travel to Canaan to bury him. Joseph reassures the brothers one final time and dies at 110, his bones embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt, awaiting the day they will be carried back to the promised land.
observation: Jacob adopts Joseph’s two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own, they become two of the twelve tribes.
Jacob crosses his hands, blessing the younger (Ephraim) over the older (Manasseh), the pattern of election repeats.
Genesis 49 is the blessing of the twelve sons, one of the most important prophetic poems in the Old Testament.
Reuben loses his birthright for defiling his father’s bed. Simeon and Levi are cursed for their violence.
Judah receives the great blessing: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah… until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.”
This is one of the earliest Messianic prophecies, the one to whom the scepter belongs is the coming Christ.
Joseph receives a double portion through his two sons. He is called “a fruitful bough by a spring.”
Jacob dies. The Egyptians mourn him for seventy days, extraordinary honor.
Joseph and his brothers carry Jacob’s body to Canaan and bury him in the cave of Machpelah.
After Jacob’s death, the brothers fear retribution. Joseph weeps: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
Joseph dies at 110. His last words: “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.”
interpretation:
Genesis ends in a way that anticipates everything still to come. Jacob blesses his sons, and the future of the twelve tribes is sketched out in advance. Joseph forgives his brothers in the most theologically loaded sentence in the book. And the patriarchal era closes with Joseph’s bones in a coffin, waiting for the Exodus.

Jacob’s blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh is the latest example of the pattern that has run throughout Genesis. The younger is preferred over the older. Isaac over Ishmael. Jacob over Esau. Now Ephraim over Manasseh. When Joseph tries to redirect his father’s hands to favor the older son, Jacob refuses. “I know, my son, I know.” The pattern is not accidental. God’s grace consistently overturns natural expectations. He does not save by birth order, by merit, by social standing. He saves by sovereign choice.

Genesis 49 is one of the most important prophetic chapters in the Old Testament. Jacob, dying, calls his sons together and tells them what will happen “in days to come.” The text is dense and poetic. Reuben loses his right of firstborn for his earlier sin with Bilhah. Simeon and Levi are cursed for their violent revenge against Shechem, they will be scattered in Israel (which Levi will become, as the priestly tribe scattered among the others, and Simeon, which will eventually be absorbed into Judah).

And then comes the great Judah blessing. “Judah, your brothers shall praise you… The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.” This is one of the earliest and clearest Messianic prophecies in the Bible. From Judah will come the line of kings. From Judah will come David. And from the line of David will come the one to whom the scepter ultimately belongs, Jesus Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5). The wine and milk imagery in the next verse suggests a kingdom of abundance. The blessing on Judah is the seed of the entire kingdom theology of the Old Testament.

Joseph’s blessing is also notable. He receives a double portion through his two sons. He is described as a fruitful bough whose branches run over the wall. The blessings that came to him “are mighty beyond the blessings of my parents, up to the bounties of the everlasting hills.” Joseph receives more, in some ways, than his fathers. The suffering son becomes the most blessed.

Then Jacob dies. The Egyptians mourn him for seventy days. Joseph and his brothers travel to Canaan with an enormous procession to bury Jacob in the cave of Machpelah. The covenant family does not stay in Egypt at death. They go home to the land of promise, even just to be buried there.

When they return, the brothers are afraid. They suspect Joseph has only been kind to them because Jacob was alive. Now that Jacob is dead, will Joseph take revenge? They send a message claiming Jacob’s deathbed wish was that Joseph forgive them. Whether the message is true or fabricated is unclear. But Joseph weeps. And then he speaks one of the most theologically important sentences in the Old Testament. Genesis 50:20: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today.”

This sentence is the gospel of Genesis in miniature. Human evil is real. Divine purpose is real. Both are true at once. The same event, the brothers selling Joseph into slavery, was both wickedness (on their part) and providence (on God’s part). The same will be true at the cross. The crucifixion of Christ was the most evil act in human history. It was also the most loving act of God in human history. The brothers crucified Christ. God meant it for good.

Genesis closes with Joseph’s death. He is 110. He gathers his brothers around him and says, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.” He is embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt. The coffin is the last image of Genesis. Not the promised land. Not victory. A coffin in Egypt. But Joseph has the eyes of faith. He knows God will visit. He knows the bones will be carried up. And four hundred years later, when the Exodus comes, Moses will indeed take Joseph’s bones with him out of Egypt (Exodus 13:19). The faith of one man at the end of Genesis becomes the assurance of an entire nation’s redemption.
connection: Genesis ends in suspense. The covenant family is in Egypt. The promise of the land is unfulfilled. Joseph’s bones lie in a coffin. But the prophecy of Judah, “the scepter shall not depart”, points all the way to Christ. The promise to Abraham is still operative. The God of the patriarchs has gone down to Egypt with them, and he will bring them up again. Everything that follows in the Bible flows from this moment.
application:
Make Genesis 50:20 your own theology. You will face evil in this life. Sins will be committed against you. Tragedies will strike. People will betray you. The Christian does not pretend these are good. They are evil. But the Christian also believes that God is at work behind every evil, not causing it, but ordering history so that even the worst events serve his redemptive purposes. The cross is the proof. The worst day in human history became the day of salvation. If God can do that with Calvary, he can do it with your story too.

And take heart from Joseph’s coffin. He died in faith. He never saw the promised land. But he saw it by faith, and he trusted that God would visit his people. Some of God’s promises will not be fulfilled in your lifetime. Some answers to your prayers will come after you are gone. The Christian does not need to see everything completed before death. We die in faith, trusting the God who keeps his word across generations.
prayerPrompts: Give God the wrongs and losses you carry, and ask him to use them for the good of others.
Ask him to make you someone who weeps but forgives, suffers but trusts.
Pray that you would hold to his promise to the end of your life.
